newsitem.title: USA: Few revisions expected for USDA world coffee data.
newsitem.headline: Few revisions expected for USDA world coffee data.

text.p: Analysts expect few surprises when the U.S. Department of Agriculture issues its updated 1996/97 world coffee production report Friday, saying it is likely to be little changed from the crop survey released last June.
"There may be some minor changes, but I don't expect anything earth-shattering," said Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes.
The semi-annual USDA report is slated for release after the close of trading on Friday, December 13, at about 1530 EST/2030 GMT.

While the December report usually contains a preliminary assessment of the following year's Brazilian crop, USDA officials would not confirm that a forecast of the 1997/98 Brazilian coffee crop would be included this time.

"Often in the past, we have put out an unannounced forecast for next year's Brazil crop at around this time," said USDA specialty crops analyst Edmond Missiaen. "It is always a possibility, but as of now we are officially slated to put out an estimate for the 1996/97 crop."
In June, the USDA said global coffee production would jump to 99.1 million 60-kg bags in 1996/97, from 86.8 million bags the previous crop year.
The USDA estimated in June top-grower Brazil would yield 27.5 million bags of coffee in 1996/97, up from 16.8 million bags in 1995/96, while Colombia's 1996/97 output was pegged at 13.0 million bags.
The USDA forecast typically comes in above those made by the trade in Brazil. Industry operators in Brazil have estimated the current crop at between 25 million and 27 million bags.
Historically, Ganes noted, the USDA raises its Brazil production figures in the December reports, but last December the forecast was left unchanged.
Ann Prendergast, analyst with Refco Inc, said crop forecasts for Mexico and some Central American countries could be scaled back after heavy rainfall and flooding in the region in October.
The June USDA report put Mexico's 1996/97 coffee crop at 4.7 million bags. Costa Rica's output was seen at 2.55 million bags and Guatemala's at 3.5 million bags.
But while revised Central American and Mexican arabica production estimates may be slightly lower, analysts forecast stronger robusta yields.

Smith Barney analyst Walter Spilka said world coffee production numbers will vary little from the numbers seen six months ago, but robusta coffee output in top Far East growers Vietnam and Indonesia may show a small increase.
In June, the USDA estimated Indonesia would produce 6.5 million bags of coffee in 1996/97, while Vietnam's output was put at 3.5 million bags.
